title: Iran says two more tankers burn in Hormuz as oil falls to a two-month low
dek: The Revolutionary Guards report fresh fires at sea, but Brent keeps sliding on hopes for Qatari mediation, lifting Indian shares. A second Indian has died after the Riyadh airport attack.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Thursday that two oil tankers and a tugboat had caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after it claimed that four other tankers had been destroyed by mines. Oil prices kept falling all the same: Brent crude traded near $93.60 a barrel on Thursday morning, its lowest level in about two months, as traders bet that Qatari mediation would hold off a return to full-scale war between the United States and Iran.

For India the swing cuts both ways. Cheaper oil lifted Indian shares for a sixth straight session and pushed the value of BSE-listed companies back above Rs 500 lakh crore. But the war's toll on Indians in the Gulf grew: India's embassy in Riyadh confirmed on Wednesday that a second Indian national had died of injuries from the 10 October attack on the Saudi capital's main airport.

## What happened

According to a Reuters report on the IRGC's statement, one tanker struck a mine while trying to cross a passage south of the strait, and a second supertanker caught fire as it left the route in the eastern part of the waterway. A tugboat that went to help fight the second fire also caught fire. The Guards blamed the incidents on ships using what they called "unauthorised routes". They did not name the vessels, their flags or their crews, and there has been no independent confirmation of the account. The New Arab, citing Iran's Fars news agency, reported that the IRGC also claimed its electronic warfare units had captured two American LUCAS drones intact.

On Wednesday the IRGC said four tankers it described as non-compliant had been destroyed by mines in a lane south of the strait that Iran has declared off-limits. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO), which logs attacks on merchant ships, has separately confirmed other recent strikes, including one on Tuesday in which two unidentified projectiles hit a tanker's engine room about 14 nautical miles north-east of Limah in Oman. It has not been established whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and by the IRGC are linked.

In Washington, President Donald Trump has kept the threat of a bigger strike on the table. "We have to do something large," he told Fox News on Wednesday, according to Gulf News, adding that it could be a "heavy hit" and that Iran "will never have a nuclear weapon". In a Financial Times interview on election night he said "there may be no reason for it". Axios has reported that he has not decided between new strikes, a deal and continued economic pressure.

## The Qatari track

Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, said on Tuesday that Washington and Tehran were reviewing proposals passed through Doha, but cautioned that no concrete progress could yet be announced. A Qatari official told Reuters that mediators expected feedback from both sides within about 36 hours. Gulf News reported that the draft sets out a three-day sequence of confidence-building steps and could lead to direct talks "within days".

Tehran's terms remain steep. Iran has said it would reopen the strait over two days if the US meets seven demands, including an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, sanctions relief and the release of frozen funds, Al Jazeera reported. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called Washington's reply "unconvincing". Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's chief negotiator, said Iran had given a "firm and rational" response and that Washington must decide whether to prevent another war.

## Why oil is falling

Brent fell nearly 8% on Wednesday and slipped below $100 a barrel for the first time since early October, Gulf News reported. It had peaked near $118 the previous Friday and settled at $103.60 on Tuesday. Traders pointed to the Qatari push, Trump's remark that he had no immediate plan to strike, and the Democrats' capture of both houses of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections; Democratic leaders including Senate leader Chuck Schumer have said the war must end and have hinted that they could use control of funding to force that.

The fall carried straight into Indian markets. The Sensex opened 1,609 points higher at 78,910.94 on Thursday, a 10-week high, and the Nifty opened at 24,378.05, Outlook Money reported. Foreign portfolio investors bought a net Rs 7,052.74 crore of Indian shares on Wednesday, their third straight day of buying. The rupee opened at 94.35 to the dollar, a two-week high, Zee Business reported.

## The cost for Indians

The Indian embassy in Riyadh said on Wednesday that "another Indian national, critically injured in the Oct. 10 attack" had died, Arab News reported. The man, from Telangana's Nizamabad district, died in intensive care in a Riyadh hospital more than three weeks after the attack on King Khalid International Airport, which Arab News attributed to Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis. Another Indian, from Hyderabad, died of injuries from the same attack weeks earlier.

The death toll from the attack has risen to 14, according to Arab News: four Saudi citizens and ten foreign nationals, among them two Indians and two Bangladeshis. An Indian from Kerala remains in intensive care in a stable condition, and another is being treated in a general ward. The embassy had earlier said 11 Indians were among the injured.

At sea, an Indian seafarer was killed on Monday when the Indian-flagged vessel MSV Al Jusufi was attacked off Oman. On Wednesday an Iranian lawmaker said Indian ships were exempt from Iran's restrictions on the strait but must still pay transit fees; New Delhi has not publicly confirmed any such arrangement.

## Background

The war began on 28 February with US and Israeli strikes on Iran. Tehran has since severely restricted traffic through Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil consumption, while the US has blockaded Iranian ports and escorted tankers through the strait. US Central Command said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil through Hormuz since the summer. A preliminary deal reached in June to end the fighting collapsed within weeks.

The fuel shock has spread far beyond the Gulf. Emirates Group reported a 66% fall in first-half profit, which it blamed on high fuel prices, and the Bank of England was expected to raise its main interest rate on Thursday for the first time since August 2023 to fight inflation driven largely by fuel costs, The New Arab reported.

## What it means for India

India imports most of its crude oil, so a sustained fall in Brent eases its import bill, inflation and pressure on the rupee. That is why Indian shares have tracked news from the Gulf so closely this week. But the gains rest on diplomacy that has not yet produced an agreement, and the IRGC's continuing claims of tanker fires show that the strait remains dangerous for the Indian sailors who crew many of the ships on Gulf routes, and for the millions of Indians who live and work in the region.

## What happens next

- Qatar's mediators are waiting for formal replies from Washington and Tehran on their latest draft.
- Trump says a large strike remains possible if talks fail; no decision has been announced.
- The new US Congress, with Democratic majorities in both houses, takes office in January.
